section_summary: Pages 137–163 contain the end of an August 1941 Radio Tokyo bulletin and most of its September 1941 issue, with multilingual program listings, transmission schedules, frequencies, and requests for listener reports. The remaining pages contain U.S. government correspondence, an analysis of Tokyo broadcasts from June–July 1941, and translated transcripts of broadcasts about Japan’s policy in East and Southeast Asia. The final transcript continues beyond page 179.

subfiles.title: Radio Tokyo, August 1941 bulletin
subfiles.about: Schedules and promotes Japan’s international shortwave broadcasts for August 1941.
subfiles.summary: The bulletin lists program highlights, transmission times, call signs, frequencies, languages, and target regions worldwide. Its English, French, German, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Malay, and Dutch notices describe news, cultural talks, and music while inviting reception reports. Page 149 is a largely illegible reverse-side schedule belonging to the bulletin.

subfiles.title: Radio Tokyo, September 1941, No. 62
subfiles.about: Publishes September 1941 program highlights and regional shortwave schedules.
subfiles.summary: The issue advertises news, culture, music, children’s programs, and features for Japanese Americans, then gives regional schedules in several languages. The German section highlights Japan–Germany sporting events, and the Italian section provides a dated daily program. Frequency tables show changes from the August issue, particularly for broadcasts to China and the South Seas. Page 163 is a largely illegible reverse-side schedule.

subfiles.title: FCC letter forwarding Special Report No. 2
subfiles.from: James Lawrence Fly, Federal Communications Commission
subfiles.to: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Department of State
subfiles.about: Forwards a report on Japanese broadcasts suggesting a move toward Southeast Asia.
subfiles.summary: Fly sends an early monitoring report and explains delays while the service is being reorganized.

subfiles.title: Copy of FCC forwarding letter
subfiles.from: James Lawrence Fly, Federal Communications Commission
subfiles.to: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Department of State
subfiles.about: Copies the FCC letter accompanying its report on Japanese radio.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate of Fly’s transmittal letter, with his name typed below the signature line.

subfiles.title: Tokyo Broadcasts to North America, June 23 to July 18
subfiles.from: Federal Communications Commission, Foreign Broadcast Monitoring Service
subfiles.about: Analyzes Tokyo radio’s treatment of Southeast Asia and the Soviet–German war.
subfiles.summary: The report finds mounting hostility toward Britain and the United States, allegations of encirclement, and stories about Indochina. It interprets those themes as possible preparation for a Japanese move southward. By contrast, it finds little anti-Soviet comment or emphasis on Japan’s Axis ties.

subfiles.title: Hamilton’s acknowledgment of FCC monitoring report
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Department of State
subfiles.to: T. J. Slowie, Federal Communications Commission
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the FCC report and requests an additional distribution copy.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton thanks the FCC and asks that future reports also go to Stanley K. Hornbeck.

subfiles.title: FBI letter forwarding translated Tokyo broadcasts
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Department of State
subfiles.about: Forwards translated transcripts of Tokyo broadcasts from July 24–27, 1941.
subfiles.summary: The FBI sends four days of translated Tokyo radio transcripts to Berle.

subfiles.title: JLU4 program transcript, July 27, 1941
subfiles.about: Reports Japan’s response to asset freezes and defends its agreement with French Indochina.
subfiles.summary: News items portray American and British asset freezes as hostile but manageable, and describe regional military and diplomatic developments. A lengthy commentary claims that Britain, the United States, and Chungking are encircling Japan and presents the French Indochina defense agreement as peaceful and necessary. The transcript closes with a talk on food production.

subfiles.title: JLU4 program transcript, July 26, 1941
subfiles.about: Records the monitored program and a request for reception reports.
subfiles.summary: Notes an off-air interval, music, a request for reception information, and the closing anthem.

subfiles.title: JLU4 program transcript, July 25, 1941
subfiles.about: Explains the nationalist message of the Kokumin-No-Sho, or Nation’s Text-Book.
subfiles.summary: A commentary describes the book’s account of a new world order led by Japan in East Asia. It calls for collaboration with China, national solidarity, and coordinated military, economic, and diplomatic action. The monitored program also includes music and a discussion of baby bonds.

subfiles.title: JLU4 program transcript, July 24 or 23, 1941
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese diplomatic and military news and begins a commentary on an alleged anti-Japanese coalition.
subfiles.summary: The news covers cabinet continuity, personnel movements, China, a planned Shanghai–Buenos Aires wireless link, talks with Thailand and French Indochina, and the Soviet–German war. It also relays a French argument for cooperation with Japan. A commentary on Britain, the United States, Russia, and Chungking begins on page 179 and continues beyond this section.
